title: The 1931-32 Armstrong tour: Texas, Memphis jail and the Northeast
summary: A long account of the Armstrong band tour, the Memphis jail episode, the Boston battle of bands and the disbanding.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: I'd never been to drugs, that's good. I'd never been to trouble. The only time I would have been in trouble, if you may recall, they put us all in jail in Memphis, the whole band. See we played, we did six weeks and when we left, see it was supposed to be a big dance here at the end of this game out there. And it's supposed to have some government warehouse or something like that. Anyhow, people came far away from Florida and Mississippi, you know, and Ramport Street and the people just, these little flippers, you know, all of them down Ramport Street. And you could see it was from out of town. Anyhow, it's a dance that was booked and never came off. They wouldn't let the people in the place. And so we left that night and opened up at Houston, Texas. We had 12,000 people there the first night and the second night, the second night was about somewhere around 4 or 5,000. So we played six weeks and then we went to Fort Worth, Dallas, Waco, and Galveston. Then we crossed over to Oklahoma and played Oklahoma City and Tulsa first. And then we doubled right back into Texas again and played the same place over. That's when we ran into Joe Oliver's band. He had a good band. Most musicians are in New York, see. By that time Joe was in New York. And that's the last, oh yeah, I did see him once in Chicago after that. So we, then we went on and we played Shreeport, it's a football game. I think Xavier was playing somebody. It's only in college, he's in Texas. And then we went on to Jackson, Mississippi. We played Jackson, Mississippi. And then after that's when the trouble began. We was on our way to Memphis, to Leroy. And there was two bus drivers, so John Collins was in New York. He was booking this RKO circuit. So the band was different charges. His wife, her name was Mary Collins. And so her and Louis were sitting together, talking business. And they kept switching on the light, on and off, at short intervals I'd say. About, they'd do it about twice a minute. Yeah, and so we didn't pay much attention to it. We didn't know that trouble was brewing. So when we reached Memphis, the superintendent there said, well, come on you guys, get out of there. So she told her, I said, no. I said, I paid, it was different than the money I paid. Because we were making this long jump from Jackson to Little Rock. And he said, boy, it's tiresome as a little cheap bus, a smaller bus, you know. So they had this hassle, they went on for about five minutes. So he told the driver, he said, well, drive on over to the terminal. So when we arrived at the terminal, it looked like half of the Memphis police force was there. So they put us all in jail, but the Vandale player, Mike McKenzie, I don't know how he escaped, because he was riding the bus with us. So they put us all in jail. So they mugged us and kept us in there about maybe an hour and we were supposed to double back and play the palace on Beale Street in Memphis. And so he bailed us out. And we had two women along with us and a guy around me called Professor Cook and Joe Lindsey. Joe was supposed to give Louis for his job. He was a drummer. And so we arrived in Little Rock about eleven o'clock that night and we played about two. And we doubled back to Memphis. The train was held up for us and we doubled back and we broadcast at the Peabody Hotel in Memphis. And here's where we were frightened again. We were playing and finally Louis said, ladies and gentlemen, I'm now going to dedicate a number to the Memphis Police Department. I'd be glad when you did. You rascal you. And so I recognized some of the policemen, you know. But they were smiling but I kind of figured it was a trickeration. I couldn't play hard. My lips was, my teeth was chattering, you know. And so after they moved the screen, they moved the screen and they made a wild dash towards us. And we couldn't run any farther and we backed up and we were, we're not going to hurt you boys. We're not going to hurt you boys. He says, we understand you're going to play a middle-drammel. So he's at the palace. We will be there. And true enough, I'd say about the first seven or eight rows was the police and the families. That midnight ramble. So we're headed for trouble again. Louis Armstrong had a lot of trouble. I mean a lot of people don't know it. I know a lot of things about Louis, I never tell. Yeah. And the first thing he had was wife trouble. He and Lil was on bad terms and it was this alpha, this, she should have been the, about the third wife. She was along with her, you know. And most everywhere we'd go, Lil would be coming right along a little later. And so we left there and went to St. Lucid in St. Louis. I remember that very well because that was a great series between the Yanks and the Cardinals, which the Cardinals won. And for the first three shows the booters and there was a whole lot of noise. And so one of the big shots came down from New York and finally things were smoothed out. And then we're on the R.R. Hill now. Then we head off there, we played the chauffeur's club. That's a great place through those days. Charlie Creff, you might have heard of him, and Dewey Jackson, you know. They were featured there. And then we left there and went to the Albion Cincinnati. Then we doubled back from Cincinnati to the Palace in Chicago, then the Palace in Cleveland. And then we started playing this one-nighters through West Virginia. I understood Earl Humphreys in West Virginia during that time, but I didn't see him. We was in Huntington, you know. We played Huntington and we played Louis Abel during Derby time. In Ohio, one-nighters in some parts of Michigan. Then we jumped from there to the Pearl Theater in Philadelphia, where they had that blue law there, you know. We couldn't start until about a minute after twelve. So they had what they called a, well it was a regular circuit. And there was some brothers by the name of the Stiefel Brothers. In New York at that time they had this old Lafayette Theater. So we played the Pearl and then we went to New York and played the Lafayette. And then we went and called it Around the World. Then we went to Washington and then Baltimore. And then back to Philly again to stand the theater. And then we came back to New York and we played in Jersey City. And then we went to Connecticut. And here comes the house again. And the old movie star, Ruth Rowland, she was the headliner. You don't understand how the headliners last. So Louis had come on right before and he stopped the show every time. See? And so she began to get angry. So then she asked for the arena so that she'd come on ahead of Louis. Well, he stopped the show as a headliner too. And so, we was just there a week and then we went up to Boston. And that's where we had the great battle with the Castle Loma and Fletcher Henderson and Louis Armstrong Band. That was right out of Boston. And that was some battle. And these Castle Lomas had the term to use during that time was cutting, you know, and whoever best the other band. And they met this great band they called the Cotton Pickers, McKinney's Cotton Pickers out of Detroit, see. They played opposite Dean Goldkett there in Detroit. And these fellas all bandaged up. The piano player had his head all bandaged up. Two or three of them was all bandaged up. But those guys really played. People still talk about it in New England. About that battle of jazz. So then we came back to our store along the island. We made a couple of shots. Well, I'll make a mouth in the shot. I'll be glad you did. You were asking them to assume he was using it, you know. And we did a lot of recording. In fact, every chance we got, Louis the record was selling like hotcakes then on an OK record, you know. So finally we were supposed to come back to New Orleans. He wanted us back to New Orleans. We had three places that wanted the band. And one of them was in France and one was here and that was in California. So he disbanded the band, Collins did. And Louis went back to Sebastian's. And so I never did play with Louis anymore. We still were friends, you know, whenever we were in Chicago. I'd always, Louis, see, by that time he had the wife that he had when he died, you know. He and Alf were married and they separated, see. But I do believe that Lil had never stopped loving Louis. I'll tell you why. You know one of the funny questions. We were in Massachusetts. I was with the Franz Jackson band. She was playing piano with us. It's been about four years ago. So we began to talk. And if you just judge the way she talked you figured she hated him, you know. So her and I engaged in an argument. I said Louis still was the best in the world. And so she said that Jonah Jones could outplay him. Well in spite of talking like that, I found out later that she just was talking, that's all. So here she still loved him. Because I found out they still exchanged in spite of being Lucille, that was his last wife, you know. When he died that was his wife. And so they exchanged presents. And when he died she flew up there as quick as she could get. And it wasn't long after he died that she died. She fell dead. They ran on the TV, had him, you know. It was one of these things. It was, yeah. It's pertaining to Louis Armstrong. I forget.
